channel.title: A Hundred Falling Veils — Poems
channel.description: Recent poems from A Hundred Falling Veils

item.title: When She Comes Home from College I Understand
item.description: Once I carried her inside me the way the sunflower carries inside it the pattern for the next seed, the next bloom. Now, I carry her the way the sky carries the moon, which is to say she holds herself in space and I simply offer room enough to stay close enough to tether, far enough to know her gravity. I carried her the way the big bang once supported the universe, intimate and everything, and now with every day she redefines space itself. I hold her the way I always have— with so much devotion and the certainty that holding her means letting her go.

item.title: On a Friday, Midday
item.description: The body wants to lie in the middle of the floor in the rhombus of late morning light; the body wants to stretch, to be leaden and long in the long bright pool of low winter sun, wants to let itself be warmed. The body wants still. Wants soft. Wants safe. Wants rest. The body wants velvety blur. But the body remembers yesterday’s grip, remembers the clench of yesterday’s fear. It can be so hard to be only here. So the mind attunes and murmurs, shhhh. And the heart hums along, hmmmm, mmmm. And the body receives the duet like a gift, like a gentle, generous permission slip to mellow, to rest, to rest, to rest as if rest is the way we heal the world. And the body relents, relaxes, receives, becomes an expression of flesh and sun, and even after the warmth is gone, the body remembers itself as home.

item.title: For When I Forget
item.description: a letter to the future self Remember the day you lit the deep red rose candle, a gift that felt too lovely to burn— but burn it you did, sitting alone, no less. In that moment, somehow, you knew you were worthy of beauty, trusted you could spend something wonderful on yourself. I could laugh at you questioning your own value, but I won’t. Having lived in your skin, I know how deep the self-doubt stabs. I know how hard it was for you to strike that match, to light the wick. Instead, I want to help you remember how you didn’t blow it out, that rose candle deep dark red. How you watched the shape melt into a rippled red puddle and found that beautiful, too. You could do it again— believe you are worthy of beauty. You could do it again— trust you don’t have to earn the light.

item.title: Well Worn
item.description: When I wear my son’s blue winter coat, I’m wearing January mornings when we shoveled snow together. I’m wearing slow drives to school on long icy roads. I’m wearing snowball fights and midnight walks and the trudge through the field to find a Christmas tree. The sleeves are much too long for me. That suits me right. I like that the memories are larger than I. I like that I will never grow out of it. There was a time when my husband said, You know, that coat is worn. Soon you’ll need to let it go. I cried then, feeling a fresh loss, one more way to lose what’s left of my boy in this world. Still, I wear the coat, threadbare and faded. Choose it over any plush new down. Choose it because it means powder skiing and watching him glide through snow laden trees. It means skating together on the ice-slick pond. It means walking beside the frozen river and watching our breath made visible in the cold. It means my boy was here. The coat isn’t him, but it’s him, it’s him, it’s not him, but it’s a whiff, it’s a touch. When I wear his blue coat, it’s like a wearing dictionary entry in which each definition points toward a loss, but the root of the word is love.

item.title: Ascent
item.description: To trust life is like climbing a mountain. The way we gain the strength to climb a mountain is by climbing the mountain. The way we grow our trust in life is by trusting life. This is the only way. Not that life gives us what we want. But with every step of every day, we gain the wounds, the ache, the fear, the love, the determination, the flexibility, the humility to meet the world as it is. World without summit, world without trail, world without map— but some guides. To trust life is to know it is life itself that climbs the mountain. We belong to the ride.

item.title: Radiant Contentment
item.description: There will come a year when she looks back and remembers how they hold each other now, arms folded around each other in sleep like four soft petals that wrap their two bodies as if they’re a single flower. She will remember how they woke each dawn like a morning glory, arms slowly unfurling in early light, how sometimes it surprised her to discover their bloom had two stems. It wasn’t always like this. She’ll remember that, too— times when every petal fell. Times when it seemed even the roots had died, and perhaps they did die when deep frost arrived. But like morning glories, the two must have dropped heavy amounts of seeds when times were good, seeds that survive even the coldest of winters. There will come a year when she looks back and thinks “radiant contentment,” words she once heard in a story about two characters who took off all their layers, though it hurt them terribly, and what was left was so gentle, so tender, so true, they could no longer imagine how to live in the world any other way.

item.title: Inheritance
item.description: for Mom on her 80th Birthday Often, it’s here, a moment when, while writing a thank you letter, or while feeling tears prickle, or, perhaps, while pulling carrots, or while singing a made-up tune, I find, tucked inside the moment, a beat in which I feel my mother’s life inside of mine. I don’t think it’s the maternal cells that crossed the placental barrier, though maybe it’s that, too. It’s more that I feel the neat, right-leaning slant of her cursive looping through my grateful thoughts, see the shining streak of her tears on her cheeks and feel her skin as mine, or remember a night sitting around the kitchen table in a long-ago Wisconsin fall as we sliced mountains of carrots to freeze. In these pauses, I feel her in me, trace of humanhood, the uncountable small and big ways she shaped my life with practicality and love. And here it is, as I open the door, the longing to find a tune for this moment and sing about it. As if opening the door is just another reason to let life’s hidden music come through me, some reprise about how, standing on the threshold of the moment, I am who I am because of her—one foot in her world, one foot in mine, and so I’m singing, I’m crying, I’m opening the door of love and saying thank you, thank you, thank you.

item.title: Through the Floorboards
item.description: for Evie She likes playing Haydn’s piano sonatas because he surprises her, she says, because his variations amaze her. I couldn’t tell you a thing contrapuntal lyricism or the sparkling details of Haydn’s inner voices, but I do know that waking to the bright flurry of joy that is Evie playing piano, well, it’s enough to make a person want to rise into this world, even knowing as I do how unkind the world can be. Because there’s this— a woman who practices every day how to coax three-hundred-year-old music from yellowing staves and make the music sing in the middle of the Ohio woods, where the leaves have mostly fallen and at the center of what is barren there is beauty.

item.title: It’s Hard to Survive in These Dark Woods
item.description: Between gray trunks and empty limbs a large crow glides on steady wings— and lifts this tired, leaden heart until my pulse is made of soar, my flesh composed of nothing more than willingness to rise—and for a buoyant beat or six, I sail, I sky, I swoop, I air, I rhyme with life, until the mind twists freedom into fear. It’s no surprise I tumble then, again a tired and leaden thing. But somewhere in the weary blood still reels the ecstasy of wings.

item.title: Mycorrhizal
item.description: for Alan Cohen and the Wellspring of Imagination And if one man should have a dream to create in the deep Ohio woods a space where strangers might gather for days to sit in a circle in a bright, warm room and listen to each other read poems, well, that is the world I want to live in, a world in which we are held by a fragile, then strengthening trust, a faith that we will be received as we are, where the only requirement for belonging is that we show up with respect and a willingness to share. In the forest itself, there are vast invisible underground webs made of branching masses of slender threads that connect the soil and plants and trees because each has something the other needs. And is our work not also mycelial? Do we not nourish each other through our differences? Do our lives not also depend on receiving each other’s gifts and honoring the wounds that activated them? I want to live in the world where this small circle expands—a world where it’s not just one vast-dreaming man, but millions of us dreaming, all of us devoted to a living system in which we exchange our goodness and trade our stories, a world where trust spreads like hyphae, constantly expanding, a world where “stranger” is just another word for a person who needs something we have to offer, a person who has something we desperately need.

item.title: One Night with Old Friends
item.description: slipping out of the straight jacket of self— what’s left rolls around the floor, reshapes itself as laughter

item.title: Twenty Questions
item.description: after Jim Moore What walls are still here around the heart? How do I tear them down? Or does the heart somehow need walls to keep it a heart, to keep it from expanding into evening sky? Who built these walls, anyway? Was it you? Was it I? Would the walls somehow be better covered in ivy and sweet-scented vines? Could I lose the walls only when I’m with you, but keep them up while I’m in other rooms? What would change if the walls were gone? Would we still arrange our bodies on the couch so close, or closer? Could you feel the lack of walls in my voice when we speak of difficult things? Would it change how my ears receive what you say? Could I love you better then? Or would the lack of walls get in the way? Would a naked heart make it harder for you to love me? Would I miss our older, more swaddled love? Could I rebuild the walls— out of what?—if loving you without them frightens me too much? And what if I find that the heart is like ivy? Something that loves a wall, something wired to climb toward light?

item.title: Shift
item.description: They’re doomed, of course, these calendula seedlings sprouting all across the garden. Because it’s November. Because even though the fall was rainy enough for water-swollen embryos to crack open their seed coats, even though there was time enough for the primary roots to push down and the embryonic stems to push up, even though there was light enough for the shoots to break through the soil, for the first true leaves to open and do their good green work of turning sunlight into food, still, the truth is they will freeze. The truth is they will not have time to bud and flower and go to seed. As I stand above the dozens of seedlings, shaking my head, I swear I hear them say, No, honey, you are the one who is doomed if you think the measure of a life depends on how much one blooms, doomed if you don’t believe that this, too, is what we are here to do: to break through the tight dry shell that has kept you safe and rise through the darkness into light.

item.title: The Day I Didn’t Want More
item.description: Strolling slow beside a slow silty river in the desert, marveling for hours at how green the land is after a month of remarkable rain. Marveling how sage brush branches bend beneath the weight of great flowering fronds. How low-angled light makes strands of spider silk shine— and the shine is all around us. It has taken me decades to want to learn what Mary Oliver means when she writes, “Oh do you have time to linger?” After scaling steep peaks and training for races, after pushing myself to go farther, go faster, after rushing to do whatever I think I am here to do, I now long to be a lingerer, a dawdler, a straggler, one who celebrates the glory in the white froth of rabbitbrush gone to seed, one who follows foam trails emerging from rapids until they disappear. I want to be the ridiculous one, the strange person staring at sky with tears sliding down my cheeks because I finally understand that whatever else I am here to do, I am also here to stand beneath blue on a November afternoon. I am here to learn loving the world is in service to life itself. That among other things, I am here to rest my body against a sun-heated rock and feel the warmth slip deeper into my being.

item.title: Being Still in the Paradox Valley
item.description: One day when I’m little more than bones and breath, may I remember this day standing at the red edge of sheer sandstone cliffs, unmoving, while the peregrine falcon made spirals at the rim— may I remember how, with no effort of its own, my heart became a fierce and wide-winged thing, carried by currents invisible and uplifting, how I circled into impossible blue, and for a moment I was only soaring heart— and that was everything.

item.title: Route Finding
item.description: How many times have we lost each other? In crowded rooms, in conversation, in movies I’ve loved that you’ve hated. We’ve even lost each other sitting side by side holding hands, close and worlds apart. Decades later, I’ve learned that the number of times I find you is always one greater than the number of times we are lost. I used to want a map. Routes change. Now all I want is the trust.

item.title: In the Attic of the Imagination
item.description: There are boxes of letters I’ve never written and thick photo albums filled with versions of me I might someday be. There are stacks of tall boxes packed with cliffs just waiting for me to fall from them and wardrobes filled with wings in every size. One corner is kaleidoscopic with blue butterflies. There are countless trunks stuffed with worse case scenarios, plus some shoes I inherited so enormous they don’t fit in the attic, much less in a box. I never know what I’ll find up here— violent rainstorms, temples of dew, the faces of the dead, red foxes, orcas, the stench of city streets or a maze made of lilac trees—and sometimes fear keeps me from scaling the stairs. But sometimes, not knowing is the thrill. And so with pencil and blank page, I climb into this place where it’s never too late, this place where anything can happen, even wild splendor, this place where the future trembles, waiting to be born.

item.title: Unconditional
item.description: What if every person knew with total certainty that they are loved and loveable? Of course, there would still be traffic jams, avalanches, stubbed toes, flash floods, dust on our wonder, ticks. Of course, we still would die, still would grieve the dead. But listen, what if all who live could feel inside us the greening, fruiting re-seeding infinity of love? Are you imagining it, too? What if we all could close our eyes and imagine the sound of our name whispered like a prayer on someone else’s lips? The world will always fall apart, but trusting we are loved is what holds back the emptiness when the bullets, when sirens, when silence, when wounds. We cannot love the whole world, but we can each love someone, nourish the wonder of their being until they see themselves as wondrous, too. What if with touch or not touch, words or not words, gift or not gift we show them the truth— that there is nothing they need to be or not be to be worthy of love. Imagine it. How might such love change the world? How might such love change you?

item.title: What the Heart Wants Now
item.description: After the long, lavish season of green, after the fleeting glory of gold, my heart is teaching my eyes to resee how the gray filigree of empty branches is also beautiful, a shrine to spaciousness, an airy splendor that rhymes with this longing to be with what is quiet, what is open, what is fiercely clear, what is here.

item.title: How Things Change
item.description: At the edge of the lake, the rocks are deep gray and unusually flat, perfect for skipping, even for a woman known for her lack of skill in throwing. There’s such freedom in breaking through an old story. On a day when so much seems fixed, beyond my control, I thrill in skipping rocks again and again. Sometimes it’s hard to see what is possible. Once, these rocks were a layer of silt. Once, this shore was the bottom of an ocean. Once, there was a girl who was told she couldn’t throw. Once there was a country with citizens who forgot how to work together. Whatever we will become is, even now, being prepared inside us. All morning, polished bits of shale fly from my hand to leap across the surface of the lake. I watch them find lift again, again, leaving rings that sparkle in the sun, a momentary proof of how sometimes the story we think we know is not yet done with its changes.
